newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan diet passes law for more BOJ independence.
newsitem.headline: Japan diet passes law for more BOJ independence.

text.p: Japan's parliament passed a bill to revise a law governing the Bank of Japan (BOJ) on Wednesday, boosting the central bank's independence and making its decision-making process for monetary policy more transparent.

"It is the greatest event that has ever happened in the 115 years of BOJ history, that legal revisions based on two pillars -- transparency and and independence -- have been realised," BOJ governor Yasuo Matsushita told a news conference.
The revisions to the BOJ law are part of the deregulation plans promoted by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

These plans include trimming the authority of the mighty Ministry of Finance (MOF) by stripping the ministry of its inspection function over the financial industry by creating a new agency and curtailing its influence over monetary policy.
Proponents of the BOJ changes have said that the old law at times left the bank prey to pressure from politicians and finance bureaucrats when making monetary policy decisions.

Analysts, however, have expressed some doubts as to whether the elite MOF, whose image has been tainted by its mishandling of various banking crises and scandals, would lose much real influence as a result of the changes.

Under the revisions which go into effect from April 1, 1998, the government's authority to fire senior BOJ executives such as the bank governor and policy-making board members because their views differed from that of the government, will be scrapped. The right to give orders concerning some of the BOJ's operations would also be abolished.

The government will no longer be able to order the central bank to postpone decisions on monetary policy. Although the government will still be able to intervene in monetary policy decisions by asking the BOJ policy-making board to delay them, the board will have the ultimate say.
The reforms also obligate the BOJ to testify in parliament on its monetary policies whenever required and to submit to parliament a report on its monetary-policy decisions about every six months.

Two government representatives who are currently members of the BOJ's policy-making board can attend meetings "only when necessary", according to the law. The finance minister would continue to approve the BOJ's budget, but only for costs other than those relating to money supply and monetary policy.

Hisashi Yamada, an economist at Japan Research Institute said that in return for independence, the central bank will be responsible for making its decision-making process more transparent, and will take the full blame for policy missteps.
"The BOJ must take into account market sentiment more than ever. I think its policy decisions will be geared more towards the markets," he said.
But there is also a possibility that the BOJ will become more cautious, as it will be held responsible for any policy mistakes.
Matsushita said the central bank hopes to start disclosing summaries and minutes of board meetings which discuss monetary policy before the start of the next fiscal year.
